Questionnaire reliability was assessed with Cronbach's α, with values ≥ .80 indicating acceptable internal consistency (Cheung et al., 2024). To characterize the acoustic structure of the 13 audio conditions, ZCR, spectral centroid, spectral spread, MFCC-derived features, and pitch statistics were summarized and entered into similarity analyses. Pairwise Euclidean distances were computed on z-scored acoustic features, and principal component analysis (PCA) was used to characterize the low-dimensional structure of the audio conditions. Given the high-dimensional nature of the acoustic feature matrix and multiparametric biosignals, our correlational analyses were treated as exploratory feature engineering to map the bioacoustic landscape, identifying primary candidate parameters for future confirmatory trials.

For cardiovascular outcomes, repeated-measures ANOVAs were used to examine changes in SBP, DBP, and PR across audio groups. For phase-based biosignal analyses, 2 × 3 repeatedmeasures ANOVAs were conducted with phase (phase 1 [p1], phase 2 [p2]) and audio group (H, N, HN) as within-subject factors. Type III sums of squares were used. Sphericity was evaluated using Mauchly's test, and Greenhouse-Geisser corrections were applied when ε < .75, whereas Huynh-Feldt corrections were applied when ε ≥ .75. Effect sizes were reported as omega squared (ω²) and generalized eta squared (η²G). Statistical significance was set at p < .05. (Blanca et al., 2023; Huynh & Feldt, 1976; Olejnik & Algina, 2003).

Pearson's correlation analyses were conducted in two sets. First, correlations among biosignal indices were examined separately within each audio group × phase combination (H_p1, H_p2, N_p1, N_p2, HN_p1, and HN_p2) to identify condition-specific physiological associations. Second, correlations were computed across the full audio epoch, without phase separation, to examine associations among biosignal indices, subjective audio feeling, and acoustic features. All variables were continuous, and all tests were two-tailed. Significance was defined as p < .05.

Results

To characterize daily stress during the 24 hours preceding each audio session, TDSI scores were summarized descriptively. Mean FREQ was 17.07 (SD = 6.45), mean SUM was 43.47 (SD = 21.22), and mean AIR was 2.52 (SD = 0.74).

Three acoustically distinct clusters were identified among the 13 audio conditions.

PCA demonstrated a clear separation between natural sounds and human voices along the first two principal components based on variations in acoustic features, classifying the 13 audio files into three clusters: (a) human voice with pitch variation (H), (b) human voice with pitch variation and natural sound (HN), and (c) natural sound only (N). Pairwise Euclidean distances further showed that the natural sound stimulus was acoustically distinct from all human voice recordings, whereas voices differing in biological sex but sharing similar pitch and background ambiance were the most similar. The natural sound file (N) exhibited the highest ZCR among the 13 audio stimuli, reflecting a higher frequency of signal polarity changes. Additional details are reported in Figure 1, Figure 2, and Supplementary S5.

Blood pressure decreased after breathing guidance, independent of the audio group.

Breathing guidance significantly reduced SBP (F (1, 20)= 14.200, p = <.001) and DBP (F (1, 20)= 7.211, p = .014), but not PR (F (1, 20)= 3.559, p = .074). No significant main effect of audio group was observed for SBP, DBP, or PR. In addition, the intervention × audio group interaction was not significant for SBP, DBP, or PR, indicating that pre-post changes did not differ across H, N, and HN. Additional details are reported in Figure 1 and Supplementary S6.

Phase effects were more prominent in BVP, SCL, and temperature-related indices, whereas audio group effects were more evident in respiration-related measures.

Repeated-measures ANOVA results for multibiosignal indices across phase and audio group are presented in Figure 3. For BVP-related indices, significant phase effects were observed for both mean BVP amplitude (F(1, 20) = 5.700, p = .027) and the linear slope of BVP amplitude (F(1, 20) = 11.757, p = .003). Among PRV indices, RMSSD, SD1, SDSD, and SD1/RMSSD each showed a significant main effect of phase (F(1, 20) = 4.903 to 40.671, p = <. 001 to .039), whereas PR showed a significant main effect of audio group (F(1.368, 26.26) = 22.76, p < .001). Additional details are reported in Figure 3 and Supplementary S7.

For respiration derived indices, RR (F(2, 40) = 5.034, p = .011) and TI (F(2, 40) = 6.125, p = .005) showed significant main effects of audio group. Significant phase × audio group interactions were observed for RR (F(2, 40) = 4.366, p = .019), TE (F(1.536, 30.701) = 4.138, p = .035), and IBI (F(1.411, 28.226) = 4.182, p = .038), whereas no significant main effect of phase was found for any RSP-derived index. For RespPRV (PR max-PR min), only the main effect of audio group was significant (F(2, 40) = 9.447, p < .001). Additional details are reported in Figure 3 and in Supplementary S8 and S9.

For EDA related indices, SCL showed significant main effects of both phase (F(1, 20) = 36.390, p < .001) and audio group (F(1.641, 32.817) = 3.716, p = .043), whereas no significant effects were observed for phasic electrodermal activity. For temperature related indices, skin temperature showed significant main effects of both phase (F(1, 20) = 35.168, p < .001) and audio group (F(2, 40) = 3.369, p = .044). Similarly, the linear slope of skin temperature also showed the same effects on both phase (F(1, 20) = 7.336, p = .014) and audio group (F(2, 40) = 5.233, p = .010). Additional details are reported in Figure 3 and Supplementary S10 and S11.

Voice containing and natural sound conditions showed both recurrent and audio group specific physiological coupling patterns.

Across audio groups and phases, several stable recurrent associations emerged (Table 1). The most consistent finding was that greater PR max-PR min was associated with greater PRV across all audio groups in both phases. Higher PR was also associated with lower PRV in most conditions, except HN during phase 2. Larger BVP amplitude was repeatedly associated with higher peripheral skin temperature, except in HN during phase 2. In addition, greater PR max-PR min was consistently associated with slower and longer breathing in the voicecontaining conditions (H and HN) across both phases, but not in the natural-sound condition. Together, these findings indicate partially stable coupling among RespPRV, PRV, PR, and peripheral skin temperature across changes in phase and audio context.

Phase-specific and audio group -specific physiological coupling patterns were observed across electrodermal, vascular, respiratory, and PRV indices.

In phase 1, greater phasic electrodermal activity was associated with higher SCL across audio groups. In the two-voice containing conditions, greater PR max -PR min was additionally associated with lower SCL, and larger BVP amplitude was associated with lower PRV. At the level of individual audio groups, slower respiration in H was associated with lower phasic electrodermal activity, including longer IBI (r = -.438, p = .047) and longer TE (r = -.462, p = .035). In N, a greater positive slope of BVP amplitude was associated with lower PRV, including RMSSD, SD1, and SDSD (r = -.530 to -.529, p = .014), and with lower peripheral skin temperature (r = -.542, p = .011). In HN, larger BVP amplitude was associated with greater phasic electrodermal activity (r = .555, p = .009) but lower PR max -PR min (r = -.579, p = .006).

Phase 2-specific patterns further differentiated the three audio groups. In H, a greater positive slope of BVP amplitude was associated with higher PRV, including RMSSD, SD1, and SDSD (r = .446, p = .043), and with greater PR max -PR min (r = .578, p = .006). In N, phasic electrodermal activity was inversely associated with SCL (r = -.566, p = .007) and peripheral skin temperature (r = -.439, p = .047), whereas SCL was positively associated with peripheral skin temperature (r = .499, p = .021). In HN, both the slope and mean level of BVP amplitude were strongly positively associated with phasic electrodermal activity (r = .909-.980, p < .001).

Physiological couplings were partly stable across phases, yet some were reorganized or even reversed depending on the audio context.

Several associations were also preserved across both phases within the human voice condition (H). Larger BVP amplitude remained associated with PRV across both phases (r = -.436 to-.546, p = .010 to .048), greater phasic electrodermal activity remained associated with higher SCL (phase 1: r = .686, p < .001; phase 2: r = .791, p < .001), and greater PR max -PR min remained associated with longer IBI (r = .531 to .752 p = <.001 to .013) and longer TE and TI (r = .440 to .716, p = <.001 to .046).

Several associations were also preserved across both phases within HN. Larger mean BVP amplitude remained associated with greater phasic electrodermal activity (r = .555 to .909, p = < .001 to .009) but lower PR max -PR min (r = -.449 to -.579, p = .006 to .041) across both phases. The HN condition also showed inverse associations of PRV with SCL (r = -.444 to -.516, p = .017 to .044) and peripheral skin temperature (phase 1: r = -.483 to -.501, p = .021 to .026), as well as of PR max -PR min with SCL (r = -.446 to -.472, p = .031 to .043).

Phase-related reversals were also observed. In N, phasic electrodermal activity was positively associated with SCL in phase 1 (r = .609, p = .003), but negatively in phase 2 (r = -.566, p = .007). A similar reversal was observed in HN for the association between the slope of BVP amplitude and phasic electrodermal activity, which was negative in phase 1 (r = -.613, p = .003) but strongly positive in phase 2 (r = .980, p < .001). These reversals suggest that some physiological couplings were not merely strengthened or weakened over time, but qualitatively reorganized across phases depending on audio context. Additional details are reported in Supplementary Table S12.

Associations with acoustic features were observed for most biosignal indices except respiration.

Subjective audio feeling did not differ significantly across audio groups (F(1.364, 27.288) = .258, p = .689) for the full audio. Nevertheless, several acoustic features were associated with BVP-derived indices. In particular, the BVP amplitude slope, PR, PRV indices, and PR max-PR min showed consistent associations with ZCR (r = -.182, p = .002), spectral centroid (r = -.196, p = .001), spectral spread (r = -.121 to -.243, p = <.001 to .045), pitch (r = -.205 to -.126, p = <.001 to .037), log energy (r = -.127 to -.216, p = <.001 to .036), and multiple MFCC components (r = -.196 to .365, p = <.001 to .046).

Electrodermal and temperature-related indices also showed selective acoustic associations. Phasic electrodermal activity was only associated with MFCC 11 (r = -.135, p = .026), whereas SCL, peripheral skin temperature, and temperature slope were associated with a broader set of acoustic features, including ZCR (r = -.164 to .304, p = <.001 t o.021), spectral centroid (r = -.157 to .300, p = <.001 t o.020), spectral spread (r = -.140 to .228, p = <.001 t o.021), pitch (r = -.162 to .318, p = <.001 t o.007), and selected MFCC components (r = -.164 to .158, p = .006 to .021).

By contrast, respiration-related structure indices showed few significant associations with acoustic features, with only respiration amplitude reaching significance, indicating that acoustic variation was more closely linked to cardiovascular and PRV than to respiratory structure. Although subjective audio feeling did not differ by audio group, it was still associated with several acoustic features, particularly mean pitch (r = .161, p =.008) and selected MFCC components (r = -.198 to .217, p = <.001 to .046). Additional details are reported in Supplementary S13 and S14.

Discussion

The present study provides unprecedented psychophysiological evidence that the acoustic properties of audio-guided interventions act as independent, potent modulators of human autonomic dynamics. Consistent with recent evidence that short-term structured respiration practices can modify respiratory physiology, particularly respiratory rate (Balban et al., 2023), the present findings further showed that ultra-short-term respiratory dynamics were sensitive to the acoustic context of guided breathing. Respiratory rate and inspiratory time varied across audio groups, and respiratory rate, expiratory time, and inter-breath interval showed phase-by-audio-group interactions. In contrast, systemic blood pressure showed a generalized pre-post reduction that did not depend on audio group, suggesting that the cardiovascular effect reflected a broad response to brief guided breathing, whereas respiratory dynamics were more selectively shaped by acoustic context. This confirms that the fundamental cognitive task of maintaining a spontaneous natural pattern of breath awareness is highly robust against structural acoustic changes. However, beneath this generalized cardiovascular reduction, our high-resolution multiparametric analyses unmasked a highly modular, acoustically driven physiological architecture.

Crucially, we demonstrated that different physiological systems tune into distinct dimensions of the digital audio stimulus. Macro-level respiratory indices, such as respiratory rate and inspiratory time, were primarily driven by the broad categorical nature of the sound (e.g., human voice versus natural ambiance). In stark contrast, micro-level autonomic tonespecifically electrodermal activity and pulse rate variability-exhibited profound sensitivity to fine-grained computational acoustic features, including the zero-crossing rate, spectral centroid, and specific Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs). This aligns with advanced bioacoustic frameworks (Wang et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2022) suggesting that MFCCs and spectral features capture subtle, arousal-related acoustic frequencies. These frequencies can bypass conscious cognitive processing to directly innervate peripheral microvascular and eccrine responses. The acoustic stimulus is therefore not a neutral instructional medium; it is an active, programmable exogenous physiological trigger. Furthermore, our intensive 13-condition within-subject design allowed us to observe that physiological coupling-such as the complex interplay between blood volume pulse amplitude and phasic skin conductance-reorganizes dynamically based on the specific acoustic context. We observed that certain autonomic associations completely reversed their directionality between the body-scan phase and the breath-awareness phase, particularly under the hybrid human voice with natural sound condition. Such profound, contextdependent autonomic reorganization has been largely invisible in previous between-subject meditation research, highlighting the absolute necessity of evaluating the acoustic context of digital interventions.

Several methodological strengths and considerations must be acknowledged. The final sample was restricted exclusively to young, healthy, meditation-naïve females. While this limits immediate broad generalizability to older clinical populations, this demographic homogeneity was a deliberate and necessary scientific control strategy. Given the high sensitivity of autonomic indices (e.g., PRV and EDA) to biological sex and age-related vascular decay, this strict restriction effectively minimized baseline biological noise, permitting the pure isolation of the acoustic stimulus effects. Furthermore, while the participant count (N = 21) may appear modest for standard between-subject designs, the rigorous requirement for each participant to return to the laboratory across 13 separate days yielded 273 high-density experimental observations. This strictly distributed daily scheduling ensured a minimum 24-hour washout period between exposures, rigorously precluding any autonomic carry-over effects or physiological habituation. This exceptionally demanding repeated-measures approach robustly captured intra-individual physiological coupling dynamics without the confound of same-day autonomic fatigue.

These findings fundamentally challenge the prevailing behavioral assumption that audio guidance is merely a neutral delivery medium. Instead, we demonstrate that even during a standardized cognitive task, the acoustic essence of the soundscape functions as an active, independent physiological driver. Aligning perfectly with the Sonic One Health framework (Pijanowski et al., 2025), our results highlight the absolute necessity of evaluating the acoustic context in mind-body interventions. Recognizing that specific acoustic parameters directly drive distinct autonomic reflexes provides objective psychophysiological evidence that soundscapes actively modulate human well-being. Such next-generation digital therapeutics could dynamically generate and adapt acoustic frequencies in real-time, tailoring the computational acoustic envelope based on a user's momentary physiological feedback, to precisely optimize autonomic downregulation for anxiety, hypertension, and severe stressrelated conditions.

EDA signals were retained in native conductance units (μS) without standardization. Because EDA integrated both slow baseline drift and faster transient responses, each analysis phase was decomposed using the cvxEDA algorithm (Greco et al., 2016), yielding a tonic component (t) representing skin conductance level (SCL) and a phasic component (r) representing skin conductance responses, and a sparse sympathetic driver (p) of the phasic activity. To align decomposition with phase-based feature extraction, cvxEDA was applied within each phase using identical settings across all audio conditions.

After each assigned audio condition, participants answered the question, "How did you feel about this audio recording?" The audio feeling scale was a ten-point emotional icon rating scale to indicate their affective response to the audio. Following the emoji sentiment analysis of Bai et al. (2019) and Novak et al. (2015), five emoji anchors (😍, 😀, 😶, 😖, 😡) represented positive, neutral, and negative feelings. Lower scores reflected relaxation or positive affect, whereas higher scores indicated irritation or discomfort.
